newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russia oil, gas seen steady despite tremors.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russia oil, gas seen steady despite tremors.

text.p: Russia's oil and gas supplies should remain stable this year, despite uncertainty over what changes the new reformist cabinet may have in mind for the Fuel and Energy Ministry, its head Pyotr Rodionov said on Tuesday.

Rodionov, whose resignation from the post of Fuel and Energy Minister was approved by President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday, said gas output from the world's top supplier would rise in 1997, while oil output should continue to stabilise.

"This year Russia plans to produce 614 billion cubic metres (bcm) of natural gas, 138 bcm of which will be exported outside the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS)," he told an industry conference. The CIS consists of 12 ex-Soviet republics, including Russia.
He said 1996 gas output was 601 bcm, and official figures put non-CIS exports at 128 bcm last year.

"Today the fuel and energy complex is in a period of stabilisation," he said, adding that despite the huge changes undergone by the oil sector in recent years, "it met all the expected demands in 1996."
Russia's oil industry, suffering from ageing fields, decaying equipment, limited export space and lack of investment, has seen production slump during the last decade or so.

Output hit 293 million tonnes (5.9 million barrels per day) in 1996, a far cry from the 1980 total of 541 million tonnes. Russia has slipped from first place to third in the world oil production league.
Rodionov gave no forecasts for oil output and exports this year. But he said that while supplies were stabilising, Russia would struggle to boost them even modestly in the near term.
"Reserves of commercial fields are depleted, resulting in a decline of oil production," he said.
"Another negative factor is a further fall in investment, which has led to a further decline in output."
Legislation governing production sharing agreements and a final list of Russian reserves qualifying for such agreements were urgently needed, Rodionov said.
Russia's conservative-dominated lower parliament house, the Duma, is holding up legislation and the list, arguing Russia is ready to hand over assets to foreign firms too cheaply.
But executives at western and Russian oil firms say that without overseas investment, potentially huge projects may never take off, causing oil production to fall further.
Rodionov called for drilling activity to be doubled, exploration to be increased, idle wells to be brought back on stream and the problems of inter-company debts and high taxes to be addressed.
He also said major investment was needed in Russia's ailing refining industry, which had also contracted sharply.
Rodionov forecast Russia's refinery throughput in 1997 at 170 to 180 million tonnes (3.4 to 3.6 million bpd), unchanged from 1996's level of 176 million tonnes.
In 1980 Russian refineries processed 325 million tonnes of crude oil, or 6.5 million bpd.
"Our refineries need to be upgraded," Rodionov said. "There is a plan to expand the conversion rate of refineries and to enhance the quality of our oil products."
Mystery still surrounds Rodionov's successor.

The Kremlin has yet to name a replacement for Rodionov, who said on Tuesday that he had heard Alexander Samusev, vice president of Rosprom-YUKOS and former deputy minister in the Fuel and Energy and Finance Ministries, might replace him.
But a YUKOS spokesman later said Samusev had declined a government offer to become the new minister for health reasons.
